01.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee
01.event: They bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori.
01.turn: The Gemara asks what is remarkable about a litra of meat, so the story is read as extravagant giving.
01.outcome: Rav Huna and Rav Ashi explain how costly it was, but the incident itself has no ending.
01.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee once bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of good family from Tzippori. The Gemara asks why this is remarkable. Rav Huna says the meat was expensive poultry or bought at a very high price. Rav Ashi says that in a tiny village they slaughtered a whole animal for him each day.
01.missing: The incident is a bare report of a practice with no complication or resolution; most of the passage is explanation of its extravagance.

02.actor: A woman holding a bag of deposited documents
02.event: The heirs of the depositor demanded the bag, and she said she had seized it from him while he was alive to collect a debt.
02.turn: Rav Nachman asked for witnesses that the deceased had claimed it from her and she refused to hand it over, and she had none.
02.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled it was seizure after death, which is worth nothing, so the heirs get the documents.
02.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the heirs of the depositor came to claim it. She said she had seized it from him in his lifetime because he owed her money. Before Rav Nachman she could not produce witnesses that he had demanded it and she had refused. He ruled that her seizure counted as one made after death, which is invalid, so the heirs prevailed.

03.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite; he had no answer and asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha.
03.turn: Rabbi Helbo could not answer the question himself.
03.outcome: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha supplied a ranked list of who reads next.
03.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite. He did not have the answer, so he went and asked Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. Rabbi Yitzchak answered with an order of readers, starting with scholars appointed as communal leaders and ending with any person.
03.missing: The passage itself holds only the opening of the question; the rest of the exchange is in the following context segment. It is a thin question-and-answer exchange with little incident.

05.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for her one-tenth dowry share of her father's estate, and her brothers said that if they had the money they would pay her off in cash.
05.turn: The brothers' offer to pay cash contradicted Ameimar's view that she is an heir, and he said nothing.
05.outcome: His silence was taken to show that he retracted and agreed she is a creditor who can be paid off in cash.
05.summary: Rav Minyumi recalled standing before Ameimar when a woman came asking for one-tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers told her that if they had the cash they would pay her off with money. Ameimar heard this and said nothing, and from that silence it was concluded that he had abandoned his view and treated her as a creditor.
05.missing: The passage opens with Rav Ashi's legal position, which is argument rather than narrative.

07.event: He visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and put his granddaughter on his lap.
07.turn: Rav Chisda objected that she might be betrothed, and Rav Acha countered that Rav Chisda had himself broken Rav's rule; Rav Chisda then said Rav Acha broke Shmuel's rule against using a woman.
07.outcome: Rav Acha answered with another statement of Shmuel that such acts done for the sake of Heaven are permitted.
07.summary: Rav Acha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Chisda and sat his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Chisda asked whether he did not think she might already be betrothed. They traded accusations of ignoring the rulings of Rav and Shmuel. Rav Acha finished by citing Shmuel that such things are permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.

08.event: He was wearing a golden cloak and sitting among Roman nobles when his mother tore it from him, slapped his head and spat in his face.
08.turn: He was publicly humiliated by his own mother.
08.outcome: He did not embarrass her in return.
08.summary: Dama ben Netina once sat among the nobles of Rome wearing a golden cloak. His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck him on the head and spat in his face. He did not shame her in return.

09.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
09.event: Rav Yosef ruled in a case following Rav and Shmuel took offense, saying wisdom is not measured out in large measure only to this sage.
09.turn: Shmuel's anger is used as evidence that Rav and Shmuel truly disagreed.
09.outcome: The Gemara suggests Rav Yosef may have ruled in a case where the woman denied her father's right, so even Shmuel would agree.
09.summary: Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of Dabil, once decided a case in line with Rav, and Shmuel took offense and sarcastically asked whether wisdom is measured in a large measure only for this sage. The Gemara uses the anecdote to argue about whether Rav and Shmuel really disagreed.
09.missing: The anecdote is only a brief proof within a legal argument; the details of the case Rav Yosef decided are absent.

11.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract
11.event: He sold rights to his mother's ketubah, stipulating he would not reimburse the buyer if she objected; his mother died without objecting, and then he himself contested the sale.
11.turn: He tried to void the sale on his own, and Rami bar Chama thought he stood in his mother's place.
11.outcome: Rava rejected this, since he took on responsibility against his own objection even if not his mother's.
11.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract and told the buyer he would not compensate him if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he came and contested the sale himself. Rami bar Chama thought he could, standing in her place. Rava replied that he had at least guaranteed the sale against his own objections.

12.event: They disagreed over whether a non-priest who served on Shabbat is liable on two counts or one, and each jumped up and swore by the Temple service that he heard his view from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; the same happened again in two further cases.
12.turn: Both swore contradictory oaths about the same teacher's words, which forced the question of how both could be honest.
12.outcome: The Gemara explores explanations and ends with an unresolved difficulty before offering a possible resolution in later context.
12.summary: Rabbi Chiyya and Bar Kappara disagreed over whether a non-priest who served in the Temple on Shabbat is liable on two counts or one. Each leapt up and swore by the Temple service that he heard his answer from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then each reasoned out his view. The same pair repeated the oath-swearing in two similar disputes. The text then turns to analysing how both could be telling the truth.
12.missing: The passage is mostly legal reasoning; the oath scenes recur and no resolution is within the segments, and most segments listed are the argument paired with the oaths.

13.event: Rav arrived at Apsetaya and prohibited its residents from climbing a tree stripped of its branches.
13.turn: This seemed to contradict a ruling that it is permitted.
13.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav found an unguarded field and fenced it in with a stringency.
13.summary: Rav once came to a place called Apsetaya and forbade climbing even a tree that had been stripped of its branches. This seemed to contradict the permission the Gemara had just established. The Gemara explains that Rav found a place where transgression was widespread and added a safeguard.
13.missing: It is only a brief precedent cited in a legal discussion, with no scene or detail of Rav's visit.

14.event: He came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees with honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats mixing together.
14.turn: He recognised the sight as the fulfilment of the verse about a land flowing with milk and honey.
14.outcome: He declared that this is the meaning of the verse.
14.summary: Rami bar Yechezkel happened to come to Benei Berak. He saw goats grazing beneath fig trees, honey oozing from the figs and milk dripping from the goats, the two mixing together. He said that this is what the verse means by a land flowing with milk and honey.

15.event: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mechoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and Rava later taught there in sequence that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and then a mamzeret.
15.turn: The first teaching enraged the many converts, who pelted Rabbi Zeira with etrogim; Rava's first teaching won him honour, but his second teaching made them say he had spoiled it.
15.outcome: Rava defended himself by saying he had given converts the freedom to marry either kind of woman.
15.summary: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mechoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with their etrogim because converts took it as an insult. Rava first taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he then taught the mamzeret ruling, they said he had thrown away his earlier honour. He replied that he had done what was good for them, since converts could choose either way.

17.event: In a case like the preceding one, Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to give a firm ruling.
17.turn: Under that pressure Rav Ashi decided the matter.
17.outcome: Rav Ashi collected the full value of the promissory note.
17.summary: There was an incident like the one under discussion, and Rafram pressured Rav Ashi to rule definitively. Rav Ashi then collected the full value of the debt document, treating the damage as that of a ruined beam meant for a sculpture.
17.missing: The facts of the incident, the parties and the case are not given; it is a one-line precedent.

18.event: Rabbi Abbahu stood in a bathhouse supported by two slaves when it collapsed, and Rabbi Yochanan went up stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi when the stair collapsed.
18.turn: Each collapse should have dropped him, but each held on.
18.outcome: Each saved himself and pulled his two supporters up with him; asked why he then needed support, Rabbi Yochanan said he was saving his strength for old age.
18.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was in a bathhouse leaning on two slaves when it collapsed. He grabbed a pillar, climbed out and pulled both of them up. Rabbi Yochanan went up stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, and when the stairs gave way he climbed up and hauled them both along. When the Sages asked why he needed support if he was so strong, he said he was saving his strength for old age.

19.event: He found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel at the entrance to Rabba's study hall and raised a contradiction between two baraitot of Rabbi Shimon.
19.turn: They were silent and had no answer.
19.outcome: They brought the problem to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved it by saying the first baraita concerned an animal found to be a tereifa.
19.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel standing at Rabba's study hall and told them a baraita that seemed to imply Rabbi Shimon allowed benefit from animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. He then set a contradicting baraita against it, and they had no reply. They went to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and resolved the contradiction by limiting the first case to a tereifa.

20.actor: A buyer of one of two small plots of land
20.event: A man with a hundred-dinar debt sold two small plots for fifty each, the creditor repossessed one and then came to repossess the other, and the purchaser took a hundred dinars to the creditor offering it to him.
20.turn: The creditor sought the second plot after taking the first; the purchaser offered to pay the debt in cash.
20.outcome: The outcome is not told in the passage.
20.summary: A man owed a creditor a hundred dinars and sold two small plots for fifty each. The creditor repossessed one plot and then came for the other. The purchaser took a hundred dinars to him and said that if the plot was worth a hundred to him, fine, otherwise he should take the money and give up both plots.
20.missing: How the creditor responded is not stated in the text shown; it is only implied by later context about the repossession document.
